title: The Philippines' mobile internet expansion is becoming a social-commerce economy, but cash and trust still structure the transaction
source_unit: Philippine Statistics Authority, 2024 National Information and Communications Technology Household Survey: ICT ecosystem / digital economy and e-commerce preliminary results
geography: Philippines; individuals aged 10 years and over and internet users across regions

observations.period: 2019-2024; online purchasing and buyer transaction ecology

denominator.unit: estimated internet users aged 10 years and over; official NICTHS population estimate

online_buying_selling_account_2024.unit: percent of individuals aged 10 years and over with an online buying or selling account

online_buying_selling_account_2019.unit: percent of individuals aged 10 years and over with an online buying or selling account

online_purchase_among_internet_users_202.unit: percent of internet users purchasing goods or services online

online_purchase_among_internet_users_201.unit: percent of internet users purchasing goods or services online

smartphone_used_by_online_buyers.unit: percent of online buyers using smartphones for online purchases

delivery_preferred_by_online_buyers.unit: percent of online buyers preferring delivery

cash_on_delivery_preferred.unit: percent of online buyers preferring cash on delivery

mechanism.value: Digital access is converting into routine online purchasing, but the transaction remains handset-led, delivery-dependent, and cash-mediated rather than fully digitized end to end

observations.method: Preliminary NICTHS 2024 e-commerce module measuring accounts, purchasing, devices, delivery, and payment preferences among individuals aged 10 years and over and internet users.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are self-reported participation and preferences, not transaction value, frequency, merchant quality, repeat use, or household welfare; some denominators differ across measures.
observations.subgroup: Philippine individuals aged 10 years and over, internet users, and online buyers as specified by each indicator.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cash on delivery may reflect convenience, logistics, or local norms rather than distrust alone; delivery preference does not establish platform dependence or reduced in-person shopping.

observations.period: 2024; social selling and digital livelihood activity

denominator.unit: estimated internet users aged 10 years and over; seller measures use the source's specified internet-user denominator

internet_users_selling_goods_services_fo.unit: percent of internet users selling goods or services online to earn money

social_media_used_by_online_goods_seller.unit: percent of online goods sellers using social media sites to sell

cash_on_delivery_accepted_by_sellers.unit: percent of online sellers accepting cash on delivery

mobile_wallet_accepted_by_sellers.unit: percent of online sellers accepting electronic or mobile wallets

electronic_mobile_money_account_among_de.unit: percent of individuals with an ICT device and active SIM holding an electronic or mobile money account

mechanism.value: Social platforms are not only attention channels but low-barrier storefronts and livelihood infrastructure, with commerce embedded in existing networks and cash logistics rather than separated into formal e-commerce firms

observations.method: NICTHS e-commerce module measures online selling for income, sales platforms, accepted payments, and electronic/mobile-money account ownership.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not measure seller revenue, profitability, repeat customers, platform fees, labor time, or whether online selling is primary or supplemental income.
observations.subgroup: Philippine internet users, online sellers, and individuals with an ICT device and active SIM, according to each source denominator.
observations.counterinterpretation: Social selling may be occasional household resale or informal activity, and high social-media use may reflect audience reach without stable business formation.

denominator.unit: internet users aged 10 years and over; source-specific denominators vary for payment and non-purchase questions

security_concern_reason_for_not_using_el.unit: percent of buyers not using electronic payments identifying security concerns as the reason

prefer_in_person_shopping_reason_not_buy.unit: percent of internet users not purchasing online citing preference for in-person shopping

not_interested_reason_not_buying_online.unit: percent of internet users not purchasing online citing lack of interest

mechanism.value: Digital commerce growth coexists with a strong in-person preference and security-based payment hesitation, so platform adoption is bounded by trust, habit, and transaction assurance rather than connectivity alone

observations.method: NICTHS e-commerce questions on reasons for not purchasing online and reasons for avoiding electronic payment; responses are self-reported and may be multiple response.
observations.uncertainty: The barriers do not identify actual fraud, platform design, price, delivery failure, or demographic differences, and the survey cannot establish whether attitudes change after experience.
observations.subgroup: Internet users who did not purchase online and online buyers who did not use electronic payment, as specified by each question.
observations.counterinterpretation: In-person preference can coexist with online purchasing for selected categories, and security concerns may be rational responses to payment infrastructure rather than generalized distrust of digital commerce.

related_sources.claim: Official PSA NICTHS e-commerce release reports online purchase/sale participation, social selling, devices, delivery, payment, mobile money, and barriers.
PSA statistical-tables page identifies the NICTHS e-commerce data products and related ICT household tables.

boundary: This record adds Philippine evidence on e-commerce adoption, social selling, delivery and cash-payment preferences, mobile money, and trust barriers. It does not measure transaction value, income, platform power, fraud incidence, cultural consumption, or causal welfare effects.
